text:
A: Hiya! Oh, you've got the same smile as your picture!
B: Hiya, duck! I'm Joanne, Arnold, near Nottingham. And look at you, your makeup's gorgeous. How do you get your eyeliner that even? Mine looks like a toddler's done it.
A: [laughs] Thank you! It's practice, honestly. And tape. You put tape here, at the corner, then draw. I'm Sana, I'm in Bolton.
B: Tape! Who knew. My daughter Becky's the same as you, all the lashes and that. She'd love you. How are you finding all these calls?
A: Good! But I'm so nervous at the start of each one, like, what do I say? Then I just talk and talk. [laughs] You talked to the Dutch man? Martijn?
B: I did! He told me about the girl from Bolton who said he should watch his daughter's makeup videos. Was that you?
A: That was me! Oh my God, he told you? [laughs] He was so serious, I thought he didn't like me.
B: No, he took it to heart, I think. He's going to try it. And he learned the word mardy off me, so he's sorted.
A: Mardy? What is mardy?
B: Sulky. Grumpy. Like a teenager when you tell them to put their phone down.
A: Ah, acha, we say that about my sister-in-law. [laughs] No, I'm joking. Bit. What do you do, Joanne?
B: School office, primary. Front desk, dinner money, plasters, crying Year Twos. I love it really. What about you?
A: Packing, warehouse, online fashion. It's okay, it's money, you know. But what I really want, I want to do mehndi and lashes from home. I do mehndi for all the weddings in the family. My cousin's wedding is coming, I'm doing like twenty hands.
B: Twenty! Your hands must be knackered.
A: Yes! And I don't even know what I'm wearing yet. I've got two outfits, one is a sort of emerald green, really heavy work on it, and one is peach. My mother-in-law likes the peach. I like the green.
B: Wear the green, love. It's your wedding outfit, not hers. Well, it's your cousin's wedding, but you know what I mean.
A: [laughs] That's what I think! Okay, the green. You decided it.
B: Glad to help. I'm useless at fashion, mind. Stripy top every day, Steve says I look like a deckchair.
A: No! It's nice, it's classic. Do you have a big family?
B: Two grown-up kids, Becky in Leeds and Liam in Derby. And a deaf old dog called Pickle who only hears the treat tin. You got kids?
A: Not yet. Everyone asks me that today. [laughs] My mother-in-law asks every day. It's fine.
B: Oh, I'm sorry, I didn't mean to be nosy. My mother-in-law used to do that and all, and I wanted to throw a cob at her.
A: A cob? What's a cob?
B: A bread roll! What do you call them in Bolton?
A: Barm! I learned it at work. And the Polish lady, Agnieszka, she says bap. And you say cob. England, honestly, yaar, it's one bread and four names.
B: [laughs] Don't get me started on what Becky's lot in Leeds call it. You're doing brilliant, you know. With the English and everything. I couldn't do what you've done, moving that far.
A: Aww, thank you, Joanne. That's really nice. Sometimes I think people look at me and think I'm, you know, not clever.
B: Well, they're wrong, duck. You've chatted to everyone in this study and made them all like you. That's a skill.
